analysis.investment_thesis: IIFL Capital Services trades at INR 313, a 45% premium to its Graham Number of ~INR 215 (sqrt(22.5 × EPS ₹22.8 × BVPS ₹90)), with a P/B of 3.46 against my strict ceiling of 1.5 — no margin of safety exists. A capital markets brokerage is precisely the cyclical, leverage-dependent business I counsel the intelligent investor to avoid at any price above asset value.
key_strengths: 7-year unbroken earnings record with Net Profit CAGR of 21.6% (₹181 Cr → ₹713 Cr), satisfying my continuity requirement
Strong returns on capital — ROE 31.6% and ROCE 33.3% — demonstrating an efficient, asset-light fee model
Finance costs grew at only 3.4% CAGR vs. 21.6% profit CAGR, showing improving earnings leverage over borrowing costs
key_risks: P/B of 3.46 is more than double my maximum of 1.5 — paying ₹3.46 for every ₹1 of net assets leaves no asset-based floor of protection
Borrowings surged from ₹292 Cr (2021) to ₹1,742 Cr (2025); D/E of 0.62 breaches my 0.5 ceiling for a financial firm whose leverage is already opaque
Operating cash flow was negative in 2 of the last 5 years (FY23: -₹793 Cr; FY24: -₹118 Cr) — reported profits are not reliably converting to cash, which is the only honest test of earning power
red_flags: Price 45% above Graham Number — no margin of safety by the most objective valuation test I know
Capital markets brokerages are structurally cyclical; the revenue decline from ₹933 Cr (2018) to ₹758 Cr (2020) in just two years proves the point
Promoter holding only 30.93% — the founders themselves are not heavily committed to their own enterprise
analysis.detailed_analysis:
By every quantitative standard I established in Security Analysis, IIFL Capital Services is priced for optimism, not safety. The P/E of 17 marginally exceeds my ceiling of 15; the P/B of 3.46 is more than twice my maximum — and for a financial intermediary, book value is the primary anchor of intrinsic worth. The Graham Number of approximately ₹215 implies the stock must fall 31% before it reaches even a fair price, let alone the discount I demand. A business selling at 3.46× book is pricing in considerable future growth, which is speculation, not investment.

The operating cash flow record is the most troubling exhibit: negative ₹793 Cr in FY23 and negative ₹118 Cr in FY24. Accounting profits at a brokerage can reflect mark-to-market gains or working capital movements that never produce real cash. Mr. Market has bid this stock up on the strength of a good FY25 (₹871 Cr OCF, ₹713 Cr net profit), but one good year does not erase the pattern. Borrowings have nearly tripled in three years to ₹1,742 Cr, and capital markets businesses — dependent on transaction volumes, market sentiment, and regulatory whim — are precisely the enterprises I have warned investors to approach only at a substantial discount to net asset value. At ₹313, no such discount exists.
